output:
# My grooming van nearly caught fire. Here’s what I learned.

Last Wednesday, I was drying Moose in a client’s driveway in Bedford when I smelled hot plastic.

It was October 28, around 2:15 in the afternoon. Moose is a Bernese mountain dog, so if you’ve ever dried a Berner, you know why the dryer was on high and why we still had a ways to go. I thought the smell was coming from the dryer motor.

Then I saw smoke coming out from under the bench seat, where my van batteries are.

I killed the battery switch, got Moose out through the side door and used the extinguisher a bit. I’m honestly still not sure whether I needed to use it, but I wasn’t standing there trying to figure that out with smoke coming out of my van.

Moose was damp and absolutely thrilled to be done with his appointment. His mom brought me a coffee and sat with me on her steps while I shook. I keep thinking about that kindness.

Everyone is okay. Moose is okay. There wasn’t a full fire. But an electrical connection and cable had gotten hot enough that the cable jacket melted back by about three centimetres, and the lug at the positive end was black.

My van is now off the road for at least three weeks. I’ve cancelled 31 appointments so far. The repair quote is $4,200, and insurance has said maybe. An adjuster is coming Thursday. Rent is due on the first, and I’m scared, because that van is my whole income.

I’m writing this for a few reasons. One is that I need to get it out of my head. Another is that Tasha is about to pay a deposit to the same person who built my van, and I want her—and the rest of my grooming girls—to know what questions to ask.

**I’m not an electrician.** What follows is what I saw and what Priya, the electrician who inspected the van, explained to me afterward. I’ve done my best to get the numbers right, but this is not a guide to repairing your own electrical system. If anything about your setup worries you, shut it down and have a qualified professional look at it.

## What was in my van

My van was built in spring 2025 by Darren at Coastline Van Fitouts. The electrical setup includes:

- A **3,000-watt inverter**
- Two **200Ah lithium batteries** in a **12-volt system**
- A high-velocity dryer that draws roughly **1,800–2,000 watts**
- A water heater that sometimes runs too

For anyone who’s never had to think about this stuff, the inverter takes power from the batteries and converts it to the kind of power our appliances use. The batteries being 200Ah is a measure of capacity—roughly, how much energy they can store. It doesn’t mean the cable can safely carry any amount of current, and it doesn’t tell you on its own whether the batteries, their management systems, or the rest of the installation are suitable for a particular load.

The cable from my battery to the inverter was **4 AWG**. Priya, from Sackville Marine Electric, told me that for my 3,000-watt inverter at 12 volts, it should have been **2/0 cable**.

Those sizes are confusing if, like me, you don’t spend your days looking at electrical cable. The short version is that 2/0 is substantially larger than 4 AWG. But I don’t want anyone reading this and assuming 2/0 is automatically the correct answer for every van with a 3,000-watt inverter. The right cable depends on the equipment, the length of the run, how it’s installed and protected, and the applicable requirements. Ask a qualified person to assess *your* system.

## Why so much current is involved

This was the part I had to ask Priya to slow down and explain.

At 12 volts, a lot of current is needed to supply a big appliance. As a rough starting point, watts divided by volts gives you amps. So:

- **1,800 watts ÷ 12 volts = 150 amps**
- **2,000 watts ÷ 12 volts = about 167 amps**
- **3,000 watts ÷ 12 volts = 250 amps**

Those are simplified numbers. They don’t include inverter losses, and battery voltage changes, so the current drawn from the batteries can be higher. Other appliances running at the same time add to the load too.

That doesn’t mean I know exactly how many amps were flowing when the cable got hot. I don’t. The dryer was on high, and the water heater sometimes runs, but I don’t have a measurement from that moment. The point is that a 12-volt inverter system running grooming equipment can put a very heavy load on its cables and connections.

I used to hear “12 volts” and think small. I don’t think that anymore.

## What Priya found

The first problem was the cable size. Priya identified the 4 AWG battery-to-inverter cable as undersized for my setup.

The second was the connection at the positive end. The lug—the metal fitting on the end of the cable—had been crimped in a way Priya said wasn’t a proper crimp. To my untrained eye, it looked like it could have been done with pliers or a hammer. Heat-shrink had been covering it, so I couldn’t see the crimp before.

That connection was black after the incident, and the cable jacket around it had melted. A poor connection can create resistance, and resistance under a heavy current can create a lot of heat. Priya also raised the undersized cable as a problem. I can’t tell you exactly how much each issue contributed or reconstruct the failure from the outside, but the damage was real.

There was also a **300-amp ANL fuse**, mounted about **90 centimetres from the battery**. Priya told me it should have been within roughly **18 centimetres**. A fuse is there to protect against excessive current, but where it’s placed matters too: the length of cable between the battery and the fuse doesn’t get the same protection from that fuse.

Again, please don’t use my 18-centimetre note as a universal installation rule. The right fuse, its rating and placement all need to be assessed for the system and applicable requirements. Priya’s repair quote includes a new fuse block and a **Class T fuse**; that doesn’t mean everyone should go buy one and swap it in themselves.

There was one more thing that made my stomach drop: I didn’t have a smoke detector in the back. There was only the one in the cab that came with the van. I smelled the plastic before I saw the smoke, but I don’t want smell to be my plan next time. I’ll be asking about appropriate detection for the grooming and battery areas as part of getting the van back into service.

## The photos that got me

Priya pulled up my damage photos beside thermal-camera shots she’d taken of her own van running a similar kind of load. Hers barely got warm. Mine had a blackened lug and melted insulation.

Seeing them side by side made it click in a way the cable sizes hadn’t yet. I’d trusted my build because it looked tidy. The cables were tucked away, the bench looked neat, and everything worked—until it didn’t.

**Tidy is not the same as right.**

I’m not saying you can look under a bench and tell whether an electrical system is safe. I certainly couldn’t. Some of what went wrong in mine was hidden under heat-shrink. But I do think we should feel allowed to ask what’s under there, how it was installed, and who checked it.

## A note about the builder

Darren at Coastline Van Fitouts built my van. I’ve sent him three texts and an email since the incident and haven’t had an answer at the time I’m writing this.

I’m not trying to trash him publicly or guess at his side of the story. I’m sharing the builder’s name because Tasha is considering a deposit with him and because this is my experience with the van he built. The points above are what I observed and what Priya told me after looking at the damage. People can decide for themselves what questions they want answered.

If Darren responds, I’ll take that into account in a future update.

## Tasha—and anyone else about to pay a deposit

Please ask for the electrical specifications **in writing before you pay**. Not just “it has a 3,000-watt inverter” or “it’ll run your dryer.” Ask for enough detail that you can have someone independent review it.

Here’s what I wish I’d asked:

- What voltage is the battery system, and what are the battery specifications?
- What inverter is being installed? What are its continuous and surge ratings?
- What size and type are the main battery-to-inverter cables, and approximately how long are the runs?
- What fuse type and rating will protect each main run, and where will each fuse be mounted?
- How will cable lugs be crimped and protected?
- Which appliances can realistically run at the same time?
- Are the batteries and their management systems rated for the current the inverter may draw?
- What smoke detection is included in the working and battery areas?
- Who will inspect and test the installation, and what documentation will I receive?

Then take those answers to an independent, qualified professional who understands low-voltage, high-current vehicle systems. I know that’s another expense when you’re already spending a fortune on a van. I also know what my repair quote looks like, how many appointments I’ve cancelled, and how it feels to see smoke coming out of the seat.

A good builder should be able to explain the setup and put the specifications in writing. And if you don’t understand an answer, ask again. I wish I’d known how many questions I was allowed to ask.

## A power-off checklist for the van you already own

This is **not a safety inspection**, and a clean-looking van can still have a problem. It’s a way to gather information and spot obvious warning signs before getting a professional involved.

Before looking, switch off your appliances and shut down the electrical system using the normal controls. **Powering off a switch does not necessarily make every cable or battery terminal safe:** some parts may still be live. Don’t remove covers, disconnect cables, touch terminals, cut off heat-shrink or open the battery enclosure. If you can’t see something without doing that, leave it for a professional.

1. **Find your paperwork.** Look for the inverter model, battery specifications, cable sizes, fuse types and ratings, and any installation or inspection documents. If you can’t find them, ask your builder for them.

2. **Look at what’s visible without taking anything apart.** From a safe position, check for discoloration, melted or damaged insulation, exposed wire, loose-looking cables, or anything that looks scorched. Don’t move cables around to get a better view.

3. **Think back over any warning signs.** Have you smelled hot plastic or noticed unusual heat, smoke, flickering or equipment cutting out? Write down what you noticed, when it happened and what was running. Don’t switch things back on to reproduce it.

4. **Check what smoke detection you have.** Is there a detector appropriate for the space, and is it working according to its instructions? Ask a professional what detection is suitable for your layout and battery installation. Don’t assume a detector in the cab will cover the back.

5. **Know how to shut the system down and get out.** Find your normal battery disconnect and make sure you can reach it without putting yourself in danger. Know your exit route with a dog. Keep your extinguisher accessible and make sure it’s appropriate for your situation; ask your fire service or a qualified professional if you’re unsure.

6. **Have the actual installation assessed.** Give the electrician your paperwork and tell them what equipment you run together. Ask them to check the cable sizes, connections, fusing, fuse placement, battery capabilities and condition of the system.

If you see smoke or smell burning, **stop work, get yourself and the dog out, and call 911 once you’re safe**. Don’t go looking for the source or try to save equipment. Only use an extinguisher if the fire is small, you have a clear escape route and you can do so safely. Otherwise, leave it to the fire department.

I also bought a cheap infrared thermometer for about $40 at Canadian Tire. I think having one around can be useful for noticing changes, but it isn’t a safety certificate. Surface readings can be misleading, and a bad connection may be hidden. Please don’t reach into a live electrical compartment or run a suspected faulty system just to take a reading. Ask your electrician how, or whether, to use one safely on your setup.

## Where things stand

The current quote is **$4,200** to rewire the main runs and install a new fuse block and Class T fuse. Parts are on order, and I’ve been told **three weeks minimum**.

I’ve cancelled 31 appointments so far, which is a horrible number to type. I’m trying to contact everyone and figure out what I can do while the van is down. Insurance hasn’t confirmed whether it will cover the repair; the adjuster is coming Thursday.

I keep bouncing between being grateful it wasn’t worse and panicking about how I’m going to pay for it. Both things are true. I’m also very grateful to Moose’s mom for the coffee, Priya for explaining everything without making me feel stupid, and my clients for being patient while I work out what happens next.

If you take one thing from this, please let it be this: **ask questions about your van’s electrical system before there’s a reason to smell hot plastic.** And if you’re about to put down a deposit, get those cable sizes and fuse specs in writing and have someone qualified look them over.

I’ll post again when the van is back and I know more. For now, Moose is safe, I’m safe, and I’m trying to take the rest one day at a time.
